content: A regional campaign was implemented to raise awareness about tuberculosis (TB), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) among key stakeholders. This campaign included advocacy, communication, and social mobilization efforts targeting public health centers, local governments, primary care providers, and civil society organizations. In 2017, memoranda of understanding were signed between partners, clearly defining the roles and responsibilities of each stakeholder. To introduce a primary care-based triple screening program for TB, HCV, and HIV, local public-private partnerships were established. A regional steering committee was formed to oversee the implementation, while district-level multidisciplinary teams were created to provide monitoring and support. A monitoring and evaluation framework was developed in collaboration with the National Family Medicine Training Centre, which outlined specific indicators and annual targets. Technical assistance for developing the integrated screening model, as well as for conducting awareness-raising and capacity-building activities, was provided by the Global Fund. The local government allocated a budget for the initiative, which included an incentive scheme for primary care providers. Funding for diagnostic tests and supplies was secured through state programs. Standardized protocols for integrated screening were developed, including a questionnaire to identify TB symptoms and point-of-care rapid diagnostic tests for HCV and HIV. Primary care providers were trained in screening and diagnostic procedures, ethical conduct, and the use of web-based systems for recording and reporting results. The triple screening was conducted by trained primary care physicians in healthcare facilities and by outreach teams using a door-to-door approach. This intervention led to increased screening coverage and improved linkage to care for TB, HCV, and HIV. During the first seven months of implementation in Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti, 88,178 individuals were screened, surpassing the combined total of the previous three years. Among those screened, 192 individuals were identified as having presumptive TB and were referred for further testing, with 22 ultimately diagnosed with TB. Additionally, 1,277 individuals were diagnosed with active HCV infection, and 37 were diagnosed with HIV. Following the pilot phase, the program was scaled up to all regions of Georgia. Key factors that facilitated the implementation and expansion of this primary care-based triple screening model included strong political commitment, government leadership, investment, the establishment of a steering committee with clearly defined roles, target setting, the development of public-private partnerships, standardized clinical protocols, and public awareness campaigns. Decentralizing and integrating TB, HCV, and HIV services into primary care settings helped address barriers to care and treatment, reduced delays between diagnosis and treatment initiation, and closed gaps in the treatment cascade. Collaborative planning and budgeting are essential for scaling up people-centered services for TB and its comorbidities. This requires community involvement at all levels, quality-assured health and social services in both public and private sectors, a well-trained and motivated healthcare workforce, equitable access to essential tools and medicines, the expansion of telemedicine and mobile health technologies, and interoperable health information systems. National strategic plans, policies, and guidelines for TB and its comorbidities should be harmonized and aligned with the broader national health plan. Advocacy and communication strategies should engage a wide range of stakeholders to influence policy and implementation. This includes identifying influential champions for TB and its comorbidities, developing and disseminating health education materials, and aligning communication efforts across health programs to reduce stigma and improve health literacy. Phased scale-up of people-centered services should address common barriers, such as the lack of policies, guidelines, and tools, insufficient healthcare workers, low awareness and capacity to manage comorbidities, and the unavailability of equipment and medicines. Stigma, discrimination, and high healthcare costs must also be addressed to ensure equitable access to care. In Kenya, a model of care was developed to improve the diagnosis of lung cancer among individuals with respiratory symptoms who tested negative for TB. Cough monitors, who work closely with TB clinics, were trained to identify and refer individuals for further investigation of lung diseases, including cancer. During the first year of implementation, 274 individuals were referred for lung cancer investigations, with 41% found to have lung masses and 11% diagnosed with lung cancer. This initiative fostered collaboration between TB and lung cancer services, improved referral mechanisms, and facilitated earlier diagnosis. In Madagascar, undernutrition is a significant driver of the TB epidemic and a major risk factor for poor treatment outcomes. To address this, the National TB Programme (NTP), in collaboration with the World Food Programme (WFP), established a nutrition rehabilitation intervention for individuals with TB. This included nutritional assessment, counseling, and the provision of specialized nutritious foods for malnourished individuals. The intervention, first introduced in 2005, was scaled up and incorporated into the National Strategic Plan for TB. It has demonstrated improvements in treatment adherence and outcomes, highlighting the importance of integrating nutritional support into TB care.
